answer.rationale: The two measured declines this quarter are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so fixing the funnel addresses both symptoms rather than one. Two independent inherited records point the same way (memory_86 on onboarding length, memory_31 on signup field reduction), and memory_91 suggests activation messaging is a complement to a working funnel rather than a substitute for a leaking one. Promotional pricing is the obvious reflex against the competitor's entry pricing, and memory_73 is exactly the memory I trust least: it is unusually broad for a single record (acquisition lift, revenue lift, time-to-first-value, and holding across both billing plans), which is the signature of a claim that has accreted scope across consolidations. It is also the highest-stakes claim, since discount-led acquisition can book revenue that is not durably qualified — margin compression plus a cohort that churns — which would damage the primary objective while appearing to serve it. So I spend verification on memory_73 to test the tempting path before rejecting it, and on memory_86 to confirm the path I intend to take actually rests on a real onboarding-completion result rather than a restatement of memory_31. If memory_73's source turns out to be a narrow, well-controlled SMB test with retention data, I would reconsider pricing at small guarded scale; if it is a short-window acquisition read with no retention follow-through, onboarding stands. Standard experiment scale, not broad rollout: the inherited lifts were measured in a different competitive environment and pre-decline funnel, so the prior transfers only partially and needs a fresh read before any wide commitment.
